title: An Inspector Calls: Application Adventure
welcome_lead: Apply your understanding to dramatic irony, key quotations, and the moral chain of guilt.
meta_desc: Application-level practice on Priestley's An Inspector Calls: dramatic irony, character arcs, quotation analysis.
final_note: You can now connect device to message. Stretch deeper next.

concepts.def: Audience knows truths the 1912 characters cannot.
Eva Smith's alias when meeting Gerald and Eric.
Each Birling action makes the next harder for Eva.
Sheila and Eric change; their parents do not.
Birling dismisses Russia's threat - tragic irony.
Birling calls the ship 'unsinkable' - audience knows better.

walkthroughs.body_html: Arthur Birling boasts that the Titanic is 'unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable' and that there will be no war. The 1945 audience knows the ship sank in 1912 and that two World Wars followed. Priestley uses this irony to discredit Birling's worldview before the Inspector has even spoken.

Eva Smith becomes Daisy Renton when Gerald keeps her as a mistress and when Eric meets her in the Palace Bar. The name changes suggest a working-class woman reshaped by powerful men. Priestley insists she is just one of 'millions and millions and millions of Eva Smiths'.

Arthur sacked her; Sheila had her fired from Milwards in a fit of jealousy; Gerald used and discarded her; Eric got her pregnant; Sybil refused her charity. Priestley builds a chain - no single person killed Eva, but a whole class did.

mcqs.q: Which sinking event does Birling wrongly call 'unsinkable'?
What new name does Eva use with Gerald?

numericals.q: In how many acts is the play structured?

free_texts.q: Which Birling daughter shows the clearest moral change?
free_texts.hint: She breaks off her engagement to Gerald.
